claim: About 8% of the human genome is composed of inactive or fragmented endogenous retroviruses (ERVs).
source: Indeed, about 8% of the human genome is composed of inactive or fragmented endogenous retroviruses (ERVs) (Lander et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lander et al., 2001.

claim: A few retroviral genes and regulatory DNA elements have been exapted to perform diverse host functions, such as syncytial trophoblast fusion.
source: A few retroviral genes and regulatory DNA elements have been exapted to perform diverse host functions, such as syncytial trophoblast fusion (Lavialle et al., 2013), and transcriptional regulation (Chuong et al., 2016; Fort et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2014; Macfarlan et al., 2012; Rebollo et al., 2012; Ting et al., 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Endogenous viral gag genes have been shown to contribute to host defense against exogenous retroviruses.
source: Indeed, gag (Best et al., 1996; Murcia et al., 2007; Yan et al., 2009), env (Gardner et al., 1991; Ito et al., 2013; Kozak, 2015; McDougall et al., 1994; Robinson and Lamoreux, 1976; Spencer et al., 2003), and accessory genes (Czarneski et al., 2003; Frankel et al., 1991) from endogenous viruses have been shown to contribute to host defense against exogenous retroviruses, through a variety of mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Endogenous viral env genes have been shown to contribute to host defense against exogenous retroviruses.
source: Indeed, gag (Best et al., 1996; Murcia et al., 2007; Yan et al., 2009), env (Gardner et al., 1991; Ito et al., 2013; Kozak, 2015; McDougall et al., 1994; Robinson and Lamoreux, 1976; Spencer et al., 2003), and accessory genes (Czarneski et al., 2003; Frankel et al., 1991) from endogenous viruses have been shown to contribute to host defense against exogenous retroviruses, through a variety of mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Endogenous viral accessory genes have been shown to contribute to host defense against exogenous retroviruses.
source: Indeed, gag (Best et al., 1996; Murcia et al., 2007; Yan et al., 2009), env (Gardner et al., 1991; Ito et al., 2013; Kozak, 2015; McDougall et al., 1994; Robinson and Lamoreux, 1976; Spencer et al., 2003), and accessory genes (Czarneski et al., 2003; Frankel et al., 1991) from endogenous viruses have been shown to contribute to host defense against exogenous retroviruses, through a variety of mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The synthesis of consensus or deduced ancestral sequences based on retroviral fossils has enabled the functional analyses of reconstructed proteins from ancient, presumptively extinct, retroviruses.
source: In particular, the synthesis of consensus or deduced ancestral sequences based on retroviral fossils has enabled the functional analyses of reconstructed proteins from ancient, presumptively extinct, retroviruses (Dewannieux et al., 2006; Goldstone et al., 2010; Kaiser et al., 2007; Lee and Bieniasz, 2007; Perez-Caballero et al., 2008; Soll et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies demonstrating this approach.

claim: Exogenous gammaretroviruses appear absent from modern humans.
source: Numerous members of the gammaretrovirus genus currently circulate in mammalian species, but exogenous gammaretroviruses appear absent from modern humans (Bénit et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bénit et al., 2001.

claim: A comprehensive catalog of HERV-T fossils was constructed in old world monkey (OWM) and ape genomes using similarity search-based approaches.
source: Using similarity search-based approaches, we constructed a comprehensive catalog of HERV-T fossils in old world monkey (OWM) and ape genomes (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to data in Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: Phylogenetic analysis of near-complete HERV-T proviral elements revealed three major clades (T1–T3).
source: Phylogenetic analysis of near-complete proviral elements revealed three major HERV-T clades (T1–T3), each of which was associated with phylogenetically distinct LTR sequences, (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Each of the three major HERV-T clades was associated with phylogenetically distinct LTR sequences.
source: Phylogenetic analysis of near-complete proviral elements revealed three major HERV-T clades (T1–T3), each of which was associated with phylogenetically distinct LTR sequences, (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Two HERV-T clades (HERV-T3 and HERV-T2) were previously annotated as LTR6A and LTR6B in RepBase.
source: Two clades (HERV-T3 and HERV-T2) were previously annotated (LTR6A and LTR6B in RepBase [Bao et al., 2015]) while a third (HERV-T1) was novel.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to RepBase annotations and citation to Bao et al., 2015.

claim: HERV-T1 is a novel clade not previously annotated.
source: Two clades (HERV-T3 and HERV-T2) were previously annotated (LTR6A and LTR6B in RepBase [Bao et al., 2015]) while a third (HERV-T1) was novel.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' phylogenetic analysis identifying a previously unannotated clade.

claim: HERV-T-like sequences are present in new world monkeys (platyrrhini primates) and documented in Repbase.
source: Other HERV-T-like sequences (found by similarity to HERV-T protein-coding genes) are present in new world monkeys (platyrrhini primates) and documented in Repbase (Bao et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Repbase and citation to Bao et al., 2015.

claim: The infectious ancestor of HERV-T entered primate germlines between ~43 and ~32 million years ago (MYA).
source: The presence of orthologous HERV-T loci in various primate species, and integration dates estimated from LTR divergence (Figure 1—source data 1), indicated that the infectious ancestor of HERV-T entered primate germlines between ~43 and ~32 MY ago (MYA).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of orthologous loci and LTR divergence dating presented in Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: Additional HERV-T germline integration events occurred in various primate lineages for 25 million years following the initial entry into primate germlines.
source: Additional germline integration events occurred in various primate lineages for the ensuing 25 MY, with the most recent integrations that became fixed in primates having occurred ~11 MYA in hominids and ~8 MYA in macaques (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is based on integration date estimates from LTR divergence analysis presented in Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: The most recent HERV-T integrations that became fixed in hominids occurred ~11 million years ago.
source: Additional germline integration events occurred in various primate lineages for the ensuing 25 MY, with the most recent integrations that became fixed in primates having occurred ~11 MYA in hominids and ~8 MYA in macaques (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is based on integration date estimates from LTR divergence analysis presented in Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: The most recent HERV-T integrations that became fixed in macaques occurred ~8 million years ago.
source: Additional germline integration events occurred in various primate lineages for the ensuing 25 MY, with the most recent integrations that became fixed in primates having occurred ~11 MYA in hominids and ~8 MYA in macaques (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is based on integration date estimates from LTR divergence analysis presented in Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: The HERV-T2 clade derives from a single, hypermutated HERV-T1 element.
source: Comparison of recovered HERV-T fossils indicated that the HERV-T2 clade derives from a single, hypermutated HERV-T1 element (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), and likely expanded by complementation in-trans.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of HERV-T fossils and hypermutation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The HERV-T2 clade likely expanded by complementation in-trans.
source: Comparison of recovered HERV-T fossils indicated that the HERV-T2 clade derives from a single, hypermutated HERV-T1 element (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), and likely expanded by complementation in-trans.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that HERV-T2 derives from a hypermutated element.

claim: HERV-T3 represented the oldest HERV-T clade in catarrhini primates.
source: HERV-T3 represented the oldest HERV-T clade in catarrhini primates, with integration dates ranging from ~8 to ~30 MYA, and had the highest overall copy number (Figure 1A and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by integration date estimates shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: HERV-T3 integration dates range from ~8 to ~30 million years ago.
source: HERV-T3 represented the oldest HERV-T clade in catarrhini primates, with integration dates ranging from ~8 to ~30 MYA, and had the highest overall copy number (Figure 1A and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by integration date estimates shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: HERV-T3 had the highest overall copy number among HERV-T clades.
source: HERV-T3 represented the oldest HERV-T clade in catarrhini primates, with integration dates ranging from ~8 to ~30 MYA, and had the highest overall copy number (Figure 1A and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1A and Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: A maximum likelihood approach was used to infer the sequence of an infectious ancestral HERV-T3 from near complete proviruses.
source: Using a maximum likelihood approach we inferred the sequence of an infectious ancestral HERV-T3 from near complete proviruses (Figure 1A and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim describes the computational method used for ancestral sequence reconstruction.

claim: The reconstructed ancestral HERV-T3 sequence had gag, pol and env genes with full coding potential.
source: Unlike fossilized viral elements, the reconstructed ancestral sequence had gag, pol and env genes with full coding potential, and revealed the likely presence of an additional open reading frame (ORF) of unknown function, located 5' to gag (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by the reconstructed sequence shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The reconstructed ancestral HERV-T3 sequence revealed the likely presence of an additional open reading frame (ORF) of unknown function, located 5' to gag.
source: Unlike fossilized viral elements, the reconstructed ancestral sequence had gag, pol and env genes with full coding potential, and revealed the likely presence of an additional open reading frame (ORF) of unknown function, located 5' to gag (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by the reconstructed sequence shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: MLV particles pseudotyped with ancHTenv were able to infect many cell lines at high titer (10^5–10^6 infectious units (IU)/ml).
source: MLV-ancHTenv virions were able to infect many cell lines at high titer (105–106 infectious units (IU)/ml, Figure 1C) while some rodent (NIH3T3 and Rat2) and chicken (DF-1) cells were comparatively resistant to MLV-ancHTenv (titers ≤ 103 IU/ml).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Some rodent (NIH3T3 and Rat2) and chicken (DF-1) cells were comparatively resistant to MLV-ancHTenv (titers ≤ 10^3 IU/ml).
source: MLV-ancHTenv virions were able to infect many cell lines at high titer (105–106 infectious units (IU)/ml, Figure 1C) while some rodent (NIH3T3 and Rat2) and chicken (DF-1) cells were comparatively resistant to MLV-ancHTenv (titers ≤ 103 IU/ml).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: DF-1 and NIH3T3 cells could be infected with MLV-ancHTenv at low efficiency when challenged with virus expressing a neo resistant gene.
source: When challenged with an MLV-ancHTenv expressing a neo resistant gene, even DF-1 and NIH3T3 cells could be infected at low efficiency (titers of ~4 × 102 and ~1 × 103 G418-resistant colonies (G418-RC)/ml).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data measuring G418-resistant colonies.

claim: DF-1 cells exhibited the lowest susceptibility to MLV-ancHTenv among tested cell lines.
source: Therefore, DF-1 cells, which exhibited the lowest susceptibility to MLV-ancHTenv, were selected to identify candidate HERV-T receptors as they would give the lowest 'background' level of infection in the context of a cDNA library screen.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of infection susceptibility across cell lines.

claim: A lentivirus-based human cDNA library was generated from human 293T cells for receptor screening.
source: We generated a lentivirus-based human cDNA library from human 293T cells, which were among the most highly permissive cell lines tested, and then iteratively challenged and selected library-transduced DF-1 cells with MLV-ancHTenv virions containing antibiotic resistance or fluorescent protein genes (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental approach shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Iterative challenge and selection of library-transduced DF-1 cells with MLV-ancHTenv progressively enriched MLV-ancHTenv-susceptible DF-1 cells.
source: This procedure progressively enriched MLV-ancHTenv-susceptible DF-1 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A human cDNA encoding human monocarboxylate transporter 1 (hMCT1, also known as SLC16A1) was identified in the selected cells.
source: Lentiviral-vector directed PCR primers were then used to identify a human cDNA in the selected cells, that encoded human monocarboxylate transporter 1 (hMCT1, also known as SLC16A1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), a 12-pass transmembrane protein that mediates the transport of monocarboxylates such as lactate and pyruvate across the plasma membrane, and is upregulated in some cancers (Halestrap, 2012, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCR results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: hMCT1 is a 12-pass transmembrane protein that mediates the transport of monocarboxylates such as lactate and pyruvate across the plasma membrane.
source: Lentiviral-vector directed PCR primers were then used to identify a human cDNA in the selected cells, that encoded human monocarboxylate transporter 1 (hMCT1, also known as SLC16A1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), a 12-pass transmembrane protein that mediates the transport of monocarboxylates such as lactate and pyruvate across the plasma membrane, and is upregulated in some cancers (Halestrap, 2012, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Halestrap, 2012, 2013.

claim: MCT1 is upregulated in some cancers.
source: Lentiviral-vector directed PCR primers were then used to identify a human cDNA in the selected cells, that encoded human monocarboxylate transporter 1 (hMCT1, also known as SLC16A1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), a 12-pass transmembrane protein that mediates the transport of monocarboxylates such as lactate and pyruvate across the plasma membrane, and is upregulated in some cancers (Halestrap, 2012, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Halestrap, 2012, 2013.

claim: Reintroduction of an hMCT1 cDNA into naïve DF-1 cells rendered them highly sensitive to infection with MLV-ancHTenv.
source: Reintroduction of an hMCT1 cDNA into naïve DF-1 cells rendered them highly sensitive to infection with MLV-ancHTenv (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: MCT1 expression in DF-1 cells conferred dramatically enhanced ability to bind to MLV Gag-GFP virus-like particles (VLPs) pseudotyped with ancHTenv.
source: Moreover, MCT1 expression in DF-1 cells also conferred dramatically enhanced ability to bind to MLV Gag-GFP virus-like particles (VLPs) pseudotyped with ancHTenv, but had no effect on the low-level binding of VLPs that lacked an Env protein or incorporated an ecotropic MLV envelope (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by VLP binding assay data shown in Figure 3.

claim: MCT1 expression had no effect on the low-level binding of VLPs that lacked an Env protein or incorporated an ecotropic MLV envelope.
source: Moreover, MCT1 expression in DF-1 cells also conferred dramatically enhanced ability to bind to MLV Gag-GFP virus-like particles (VLPs) pseudotyped with ancHTenv, but had no effect on the low-level binding of VLPs that lacked an Env protein or incorporated an ecotropic MLV envelope (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by VLP binding assay data shown in Figure 3.

claim: MCT1 was likely the receptor used by HERV-T to infect ancient old world primates.
source: Thus, MCT1 was likely the receptor used by HERV-T to infect ancient old world primates.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the functional data showing MCT1 confers susceptibility to ancHTenv-pseudotyped viruses.

claim: The modern human genome harbors a single HERV-T provirus that includes an env gene with nearly full coding potential.
source: Notably, the modern human genome harbors a single HERV-T provirus that includes an env gene with nearly full coding potential (de Parseval et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to de Parseval et al., 2003.

claim: The HERV-T env ORF in the modern human genome lacks only five amino acids at the C-terminus.
source: This env ORF lacks only five amino acids at the C-terminus, shares 86% amino acid identity with the reconstructed ancHTenv and is expressed mainly in healthy thyroid tissue (de Parseval et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to de Parseval et al., 2003.

claim: The HERV-T env in the modern human genome shares 86% amino acid identity with the reconstructed ancHTenv.
source: This env ORF lacks only five amino acids at the C-terminus, shares 86% amino acid identity with the reconstructed ancHTenv and is expressed mainly in healthy thyroid tissue (de Parseval et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is based on sequence comparison between hsaHTenv and ancHTenv.

claim: The HERV-T env in the modern human genome is expressed mainly in healthy thyroid tissue.
source: This env ORF lacks only five amino acids at the C-terminus, shares 86% amino acid identity with the reconstructed ancHTenv and is expressed mainly in healthy thyroid tissue (de Parseval et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to de Parseval et al., 2003.

claim: The HERV-T provirus containing hsaHTenv is present at the orthologous site in gorilla and orangutan genomes.
source: The provirus is also present at the orthologous site in gorilla and orangutan genomes, but absent in chimpanzees due to a segmental deletion at that locus.
evidence: The claim is based on comparative genomic analysis.

claim: The HERV-T provirus containing hsaHTenv is absent in chimpanzees due to a segmental deletion at that locus.
source: The provirus is also present at the orthologous site in gorilla and orangutan genomes, but absent in chimpanzees due to a segmental deletion at that locus.
evidence: The claim is based on comparative genomic analysis.

claim: The HERV-T provirus containing hsaHTenv originated from bona-fide retroviral integration (presence of a 4 bp target site duplication).
source: This provirus originated from bona-fide retroviral integration (presence of a 4 bp target site duplication) into the internal sequence of another HERV (Repbase: HERVIP10FH), in a locus surrounded by other repetitive sequence elements.
evidence: The claim is based on identification of a target site duplication, a hallmark of retroviral integration.

claim: The HERV-T provirus containing hsaHTenv integrated into the internal sequence of another HERV (Repbase: HERVIP10FH).
source: This provirus originated from bona-fide retroviral integration (presence of a 4 bp target site duplication) into the internal sequence of another HERV (Repbase: HERVIP10FH), in a locus surrounded by other repetitive sequence elements.
evidence: The claim is based on genomic sequence analysis.

claim: Sequence similarity searches using the env region suggested the absence of an orthologous insertion in non-hominid primate genomes.
source: Sequence similarity searches using the env region suggested the absence of an orthologous insertion in non-hominid primate genomes.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence similarity searches.

claim: The divergence between the paired LTRs of the provirus containing hsaHTenv gave an estimated integration date of ~7–19 million years ago.
source: Moreover, the divergence between the paired LTRs of this provirus gave an estimated integration date of ~7–19 MYA (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is based on LTR divergence analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: The provirus containing hsaHTenv was inserted into the germline of the ancestor of modern hominids at least ~13–19 million years ago.
source: Adjustment of this estimate to account for species distribution leads to the conclusion that this provirus was inserted into the germline of the ancestor of modern hominids at least ~13–19 MYA.
evidence: The claim is based on adjustment of LTR divergence estimates to account for species distribution.

claim: hsaHTenv was not able to generate infectious pseudotyped MLV particles.
source: Unlike the reconstructed ancHTenv, the Env protein product of the modern human HERV-T provirus (hsaHTenv) was not able to generate infectious pseudotyped MLV particles (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: hsaHTenv-HA protein was not correctly processed.
source: Moreover, unlike ancHTenv-HA, the hsaHTenv-HA protein was not correctly processed and was not incorporated into viral particles (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: hsaHTenv-HA protein was not incorporated into viral particles.
source: Moreover, unlike ancHTenv-HA, the hsaHTenv-HA protein was not correctly processed and was not incorporated into viral particles (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: ancHTenv expression was able to drive syncytium formation.
source: Furthermore, while ancHTenv expression was able to drive syncytium formation, hsaHTenv had no fusogenic activity (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell fusion assay data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: hsaHTenv had no fusogenic activity.
source: Furthermore, while ancHTenv expression was able to drive syncytium formation, hsaHTenv had no fusogenic activity (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell fusion assay data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: hsaHTenv and orthologous env sequences in gorillas and orangutans have mutations at the site where proteolytic cleavage by furin-like proteases generates surface (SU) and transmembrane (TM) subunits.
source: Inspection of the hsaHTenv and orthologous env sequences in gorillas and orangutans revealed mutations at the site where proteolytic cleavage by furin-like proteases generates surface (SU) and transmembrane (TM) subunits (Hallenberger et al., 1992) (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 4E and citation to Hallenberger et al., 1992.

claim: Insertion of furin cleavage site mutations into ancHTenv abolished cleavage and pseudotype infection.
source: Insertion of these cleavage site mutations into ancHTenv abolished cleavage and pseudotype infection, while reversion of mutations in hsaHTenv did not correct the cleavage defect and did not yield infectious MLV particles (Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Reversion of furin cleavage site mutations in hsaHTenv did not correct the cleavage defect and did not yield infectious MLV particles.
source: Insertion of these cleavage site mutations into ancHTenv abolished cleavage and pseudotype infection, while reversion of mutations in hsaHTenv did not correct the cleavage defect and did not yield infectious MLV particles (Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loss of HERV-T envelope function by hsaHTenv was a multi-step process, including loss of furin cleavability.
source: Thus, loss of HERV-T envelope function by hsaHTenv was a multi-step process, including loss of furin cleavability, similar to findings with feline endogenous retroviral Env proteins (Ito et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that reverting furin site mutations alone did not restore function, and is supported by citation to Ito et al., 2016.

claim: Only 6% of simulated sequences maintained the env ORF following simulated neutral evolution for 13–19 million years.
source: Only 6% of sequences maintained the env ORF following simulated neutral evolution for 13–19 MY (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Monte-Carlo simulation results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 6% represents an overestimate of ORF preservation under neutral evolution as indels were not simulated.
source: Note that 6% represents an overestimate as indels were not simulated.
evidence: The claim is an inference about the limitations of the simulation.

claim: Orthologous human and orangutan proviruses revealed highly selective preservation of the env ORF.
source: Strikingly, inspection of orthologous human and orangutan proviruses revealed highly selective preservation of the env ORF, while numerous stop codons (6 to 16) and frameshifts (3 to 5) were present in gag and pol genes of the same provirus (Figure 5B and Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B and Table 2.

claim: Numerous stop codons (6 to 16) and frameshifts (3 to 5) were present in gag and pol genes of the provirus containing hsaHTenv.
source: Strikingly, inspection of orthologous human and orangutan proviruses revealed highly selective preservation of the env ORF, while numerous stop codons (6 to 16) and frameshifts (3 to 5) were present in gag and pol genes of the same provirus (Figure 5B and Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B and Table 2.

claim: For the gorilla provirus, a single nucleotide frameshift was the only lesion in env, suggesting recent inactivation.
source: For the gorilla provirus, a single nucleotide frameshift was the only lesion in env, suggesting recent inactivation.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis and represents an inference about the timing of inactivation.

claim: The human and orangutan env genes show signatures of purifying selection (dN/dS ≈ 0.5, p<0.01).
source: Pairwise sequence comparisons revealed that the human and orangutan env genes show signatures of purifying selection (dN/dS ≈ 0.5, p<0.01), whereas comparisons with the gorilla env suggest a relaxed selection (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by dN/dS analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Comparisons with the gorilla env suggest a relaxed selection.
source: Pairwise sequence comparisons revealed that the human and orangutan env genes show signatures of purifying selection (dN/dS ≈ 0.5, p<0.01), whereas comparisons with the gorilla env suggest a relaxed selection (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by dN/dS analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Selective pressures appear to have preserved the HERV-T env ORF despite the loss of its retroviral envelope function.
source: Overall, selective pressures appear to have preserved this HERV-T env ORF despite the loss of its retroviral envelope function, and numerous inactivating mutations in the accompanying gag and pol genes.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the dN/dS analysis and comparison with gag/pol inactivation.

claim: hsaHTenv and ancHTenv16MYA inhibited MLV-ancHTenv infection by >10 fold in 293T cells and DF-1 cells expressing hMCT1-HA.
source: Strikingly, hsaHTenv and ancHTenv16MYA inhibited MLV-ancHTenv infection by >10 fold in both cell lines (Figure 6B and C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B, C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: 293T cell clones stably expressing hsaHTenv were ~50–100-fold less susceptible to MLV-ancHTenv as compared to control cells.
source: Cell clones (293T) stably expressing hsaHTenv were ~50–100-fold less susceptible to MLV-ancHTenv as compared to control cells, but fully susceptible to amphotropic MLV infection (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: 293T cell clones stably expressing hsaHTenv were fully susceptible to amphotropic MLV infection.
source: Cell clones (293T) stably expressing hsaHTenv were ~50–100-fold less susceptible to MLV-ancHTenv as compared to control cells, but fully susceptible to amphotropic MLV infection (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: hsaHTenv, ancHTenv16MYA or ancHTenv expression caused depletion of endogenous MCT1 in 293T cells.
source: Western blot analyses showed that hsaHTenv, ancHTenv16MYA or ancHTenv expression caused depletion of endogenous MCT1 in 293T cells (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Expression of hsaHTenv-HA, ancHTenv-HA or ancHTenv16MYA-HA clearly depleted Flag-tagged hMCT1 from the surface of nearly all DF-1 cells examined.
source: In DF-1 cells, expression of hsaHTenv-HA, ancHTenv-HA or ancHTenv16MYA-HA clearly depleted Flag-tagged hMCT1 from the surface of nearly all cells examined (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the majority of hsaHTenv-HA, ancHTenv-HA or ancHTenv16MYA-HA expressing DF-1 cells, MCT1-FLAG immunofluorescence was nearly undetectable.
source: In the majority of hsaHTenv-HA, ancHTenv-HA or ancHTenv16MYA-HA expressing DF-1 cells, MCT1-FLAG immunofluorescence was nearly undetectable while a few cells showed low levels of intracellular staining (a mixture of diffuse and punctate MCT1-FLAG staining) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: A few hsaHTenv-HA, ancHTenv-HA or ancHTenv16MYA-HA expressing DF-1 cells showed low levels of intracellular MCT1-FLAG staining (a mixture of diffuse and punctate staining).
source: In the majority of hsaHTenv-HA, ancHTenv-HA or ancHTenv16MYA-HA expressing DF-1 cells, MCT1-FLAG immunofluorescence was nearly undetectable while a few cells showed low levels of intracellular staining (a mixture of diffuse and punctate MCT1-FLAG staining) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: ancHTenv16MYA and hsaHTenv exhibit antiviral activity specifically against HERV-T by causing a reduction in the levels of MCT1 at the cell surface.
source: Thus, these data collectively suggest that ancHTenv16MYA and hsaHTenv exhibit antiviral activity specifically against HERV-T by causing a reduction in the levels of MCT1 at the cell surface.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the infection inhibition and MCT1 depletion data.

claim: HERV-T began to infiltrate primate germ lines, using MCT1 as a receptor ~43–32 million years ago.
source: These findings suggest a scenario in which HERV-T began to infiltrate primate germ lines, using MCT1 as a receptor ~43–32 MYA.
evidence: The claim is a synthesis of the dating and receptor identification data.

claim: A HERV-T Env sequence (represented approximately by ancHTenv16MYA) was exapted by ancestral hominids ~19–13 million years ago to serve as an antiviral gene.
source: Later, ~19–13 MYA, a HERV-T Env sequence (represented approximately by ancHTenv16MYA) was exapted by ancestral hominids and to serve as an antiviral gene.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the dating, selective preservation, and antiviral activity data.

claim: AncHTenv16MYA apparently functioned by interacting with MCT1, either at the cell surface promoting its internalization, or in the secretory pathway, blocking its transport to the plasma membrane, leading to MCT1 degradation and its depletion from the cell surface.
source: AncHTenv16MYA apparently functioned by interacting with MCT1, either at the cell surface promoting its internalization, or in the secretory pathway, blocking its transport to the plasma membrane, leading to MCT1 degradation and its depletion from the cell surface.

claim: The mechanism of MCT1 depletion by ancHTenv16MYA is analogous to the specific receptor interference phenomena observed in retroviral infections.
source: This process is analogous to the specific receptor interference phenomena observed in retroviral infections (Nethe et al., 2005) and exploited by endogenous env genes that exhibit antiviral activity in other species (Gardner et al., 1991; Ito et al., 2013; Kozak, 2015; Robinson and Lamoreux, 1976; Spencer et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies of receptor interference.

claim: The progenitor of hsaHTenv would have imposed a fitness cost on its ancestral hominid host given the fusogenic potential of ancHTenv.
source: Given the fusogenic potential of ancHTenv, it is likely that the progenitor of hsaHTenv would have imposed a fitness cost on its ancestral hominid host.

claim: The progenitor of hsaHTenv acquired mutations either concurrent with, or after, its integration that resulted in loss of its fusogenic potential (e.g. furin cleavage site mutations).
source: We speculate that the progenitor of hsaHTenv acquired mutations either concurrent with, or after, its integration that resulted in loss of its fusogenic potential (e.g. furin cleavage site mutations).

source: Indeed, it is plausible that this exapted gene might have contributed to the apparent extinction of HERV-T from hominids at some point after the deposition of the most recent fixed hominid germline insertion, ~11 MYA.

claim: The selection pressures acting on hsaHTenv, its orthologs and progenitors might have been complex.

claim: A relaxation of selective forces might be expected to have occurred after HERV-T extinction, perhaps leading to reduced antiviral activity observed in modern hsaHTenv.
source: Moreover, although some purifying selective pressure (low dN/dS) can be detected in hsaHTenv and its orangutan ortholog, a relaxation of those forces might be expected to have occurred after HERV-T extinction, perhaps leading to reduced antiviral activity observed in modern hsaHTenv.

claim: The ability of hsaHTenv to deplete MCT1 from cell surfaces may suggest an additional or alternative metabolism-related cellular or even anti-tumor functions and selective pressures.
source: Finally, as MCT-1 is a moncaboxylate transporter that is upregulated in human cancers (Halestrap, 2013), the ability of hsaHTenv to deplete MCT1 from cell surfaces may suggest an additional or alternative metabolism-related cellular or even anti-tumor functions and selective pressures.
evidence: The claim is a speculative inference by the authors, supported by citation to Halestrap, 2013.

source: Construction of a near-complete catalog of HERV-T fossils in primate genomes allowed us to estimate a ~32 MY old ancestral sequence and reconstruct a functional envelope protein (ancHTenv) that could support infection of a pseudotyped modern gammaretrovirus.

claim: Monocarboxylate transporter-1 (MCT-1) is a receptor used by HERV-T for attachment and infection.
source: Using ancHTenv, we identify monocarboxylate transporter-1 (MCT-1) as a receptor used by HERV-T for attachment and infection.

source: A single HERV-T provirus in hominid genomes includes an env gene (hsaHTenv) that has been uniquely preserved.
